fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: Turn a Problem into a Question
fields.content:
A local grievance concerns a problem experienced or reported in a particular place. To investigate it, identify who raised the concern, which rule or action it involved, and what change was requested. A general label such as unfairness is a starting point, not a complete explanation. Ask what evidence gives the complaint its specific meaning.

Use this fictional classroom example: a reading club says that one rule keeps some members from borrowing books. The club asks who made the rule and how it might be changed. This connects a practical problem with questions about authority and participation. It is a teaching example, not a historical petition. Historical grievances need their own records. A complaint may challenge one rule without rejecting every institution. Political awareness in this mission means thinking about rules, authority and participation; it is not a claim that everyone already supported one national program.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

fields.title: A Petition Asked an Authority to Act
fields.content:
Revisit Bacolor, Pampanga, as an earlier comparison. In 1698, Chinese mestizo chiefs petitioned the colonial government for relief from tribute-collection duties. The UP Diliman research summary connects their request with financial pressure from a land-regularization policy. In simple terms, that policy required payment to make landholding legally recognized. Keep the particular request and the people named by the source together.

The year 1698 is in the 17th century. This flashback shows that people could question burdens before the later international documents in Mission 3. It does not establish that they used those later texts or held every later political idea. A formal request was a way to address an authority; it was not the same action as an armed uprising. A petition also does not prove that its demands were granted. Do not assign a common motive to everyone from ancestry or a category label. Use the reported action and concern as your evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

fields.title: Production Rules Could Raise Complaints
fields.content:
The government tobacco monopoly, established in 1782, connects the reform questions in Mission 2 with local burdens. The National Tobacco Administration account describes compulsory planting, production quotas and complaints in affected areas. A quota could place a demand on producers even when officials described a policy as a way to raise government income. This is a connection between a rule and a reported difficulty, not proof that everyone had the same experience.

Ask a precise question: What did the policy require, and whose account describes its effects? A government income record and a producers account can concern the same system while answering different questions. Compare them rather than treating income as every households wellbeing. Do not assume that every region grew the crop or every complaint had the same outcome. Tobacco appears only as historical evidence. This activity does not ask you to grow, buy or use it. Your task is to explain the relationship between policy and a supported concern.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

fields.title: Basi: A Local Product and Colonial Control
fields.content:
The Basi Revolt in Ilocos in 1807 opposed a government monopoly over basi, a sugarcane wine. The CCP account connects the policy with official control over makers and selling prices. A local product could therefore become part of a dispute about economic choices and colonial authority. Identify the policy connection rather than reducing the concern to a dislike of one official or guessing every persons private motive.

This case also helps distinguish forms of response. A petition is a formal request; the Basi case was an uprising. Similar concerns about burdens do not make the two actions identical or show that their participants coordinated a shared program. Keep the cases separate before comparing them. Basi is discussed as a historical product, not an invitation to make or drink alcohol. We do not reenact violence or award points for harm. Your investigation asks which evidence links a particular concern with a particular action, and what still needs more evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

fields.title: Explain Awareness Without Guessing
fields.content:
A recorded request can show people addressing authority about a concern. A reported uprising can show opposition to a policy. These are ways to investigate political awareness through actions and arguments. They do not reveal every private belief. To explain growing awareness over time, compare several dated records and ask what changed in the concerns expressed, the audiences addressed or the forms of participation.

One source cannot prove that everyone became aware at the same moment. Shared grievances do not automatically mean a shared national identity or a coordinated national plan. International writings could offer ideas to discuss, but claims about influence need evidence of receipt and response, as you learned in Mission 3. Local experiences also matter. Build a report with one supported connection and one honest limit. For example, distinguish a request for relief from a demand for complete independence. The next chapter will examine national consciousness more closely using its own evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.
